title: Everest Base Camp Trek: Full Guide
excerpt: The complete guide to the Everest Base Camp trek: the route day by day, acclimatization, the Lukla flight, permits, seasons, fitness and cost.
seoTitle: Everest Base Camp Trek Guide: Route, Cost and Best Season

content.value: In the first light of morning, on Kala Patthar at 5,545 m (18,192 ft), Everest stands before you at its full height, 8,848 m, as close as few people ever see it. The Everest Base Camp trek is a walking journey through the Khumbu valley in eastern Nepal to the base camp of the highest mountain in the world, at 5,364 m (17,598 ft). It requires no technical climbing experience, but it does require good fitness, about two weeks of walking and patience with the acclimatization process. The recommended seasons are spring and fall, before and after the monsoon.

It is one of the best-known treks in the world, and in peak season about a thousand trekkers a day enter Sagarmatha National Park. Even so, many set out without fully knowing what awaits them: how many days are really needed, why altitude sets the pace, how to reach Lukla and what the price includes. This guide answers those questions. It is based on the trek we run, the 19-day Everest Base Camp and Gokyo trek, which adds Kala Patthar, the Cho La pass and the Gokyo Lakes to Base Camp.

content.value: What the Everest Base Camp trek actually is

The trek starts in Lukla, a village at 2,860 m that is home to the airport of the Everest region. From there you walk up the Dudh Koshi river valley to Namche Bazaar, the Sherpa market town, and continue through Tengboche, Dingboche and Lobuche to Gorak Shep, the last overnight stop before Base Camp. There are no roads between Lukla and Base Camp. You move on foot, sleep in teahouses along the trail, and the large bags go up with the porters.

Most of the route lies within Sagarmatha National Park, which bears the Nepali name of Everest and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Dudh Koshi valley is the home of Sherpa culture, and some of the greatest climbers in the history of Everest came from the Sherpa community. We have written separately about one of them, Kami Rita Sherpa, who has reached the summit 32 times.

The classic route goes up to Base Camp and comes down the same way. Our route makes a loop: after Base Camp and Kala Patthar it crosses west over the Cho La pass into the Gokyo valley, and descends to Namche through a different valley. That way you see two valleys instead of one, and reach two viewpoints over Everest: Kala Patthar and Gokyo Ri.

content.value: Our route, day by day
This is how HighAir's Everest Base Camp and Gokyo trek is built. The altitudes in brackets are those of the overnight stop or of the high point of that day:

items: Day 1: arrival in Kathmandu and transfer to the hotel.
Day 2: preparation day in Kathmandu, a briefing with the local guides and a gear check.
Day 3: helicopter flight to Lukla (2,860 m) and a walk to Phakding (2,610 m).
Day 4: up to Namche Bazaar (3,440 m), over the Hillary suspension bridge above the Dudh Koshi river.
Day 5: acclimatization day in Namche Bazaar, with a short walk to a viewpoint.
Day 6: Tengboche (3,860 m) and its old monastery.
Day 9: Lobuche (4,940 m), past the memorials to climbers who died in the area.
Day 10: Everest Base Camp (5,364 m) and down to sleep at Gorak Shep (5,140 m).
Day 11: early climb to Kala Patthar (5,545 m) for sunrise facing Everest, and down to Dzongla (4,830 m).
Day 12: crossing the Cho La pass (5,420 m) and down to Thagnak (4,700 m).
Day 13: up Gokyo Ri (5,360 m) and overnight in Gokyo village (4,750 m).
Day 15: a long descent to Namche Bazaar (3,440 m).
Day 16: the last walking day, to Lukla, and a farewell dinner with the guides and porters.
Day 17: helicopter flight back to Kathmandu.
Day 18: spare day in case of bad weather, or a free day in Kathmandu.
Day 19: transfer to the airport and flight home.

content.value: Walking days last between 3 and 11 hours, and distances range from 2 to 16 km a day. The longest walking day is the Cho La crossing, about 10 to 11 hours. On paper the distances are not great, but at this altitude every kilometer asks more of you.

content.title: ✦ Two acclimatization days and a spare day
content.value: Two days in the schedule are dedicated to acclimatization, in Namche Bazaar and Dingboche, and on them you sleep at the same altitude as the night before. Day 18 is a spare day in Kathmandu, in case the weather delays the flight from Lukla.

content.value: Acclimatization: why altitude sets the pace

The main risk on this trek is not technical but physiological. The higher you go, the less oxygen each breath brings in, and the body needs time to adapt. The Everest Base Camp trek reaches altitudes where acclimatization is the main thing.

The accepted rule in mountain medicine is clear: above 3,000 m, do not raise your sleeping altitude by more than 500 m a night, and add an extra night of acclimatization for every 1,000 m of sleeping altitude gained. For some people even this pace is too fast, so listen to your body.

Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. When symptoms get worse despite rest at the same altitude, you descend. That is our rule: if altitude makes continuing unsafe, descent is immediate. The altitude sickness protocol is explained to all participants in advance, and every group carries a pulse oximeter and a dedicated satellite device.

Our route is built around this principle. After the first night in Namche comes an acclimatization day, and after Dingboche comes another. Even on the high days you climb high and sleep lower: from Base Camp, 5,364 m, you descend to sleep at Gorak Shep, and from Kala Patthar, 5,545 m, you descend to Dzongla, 4,830 m. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching the goal, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.
Life in the teahouses

Throughout the trek you sleep in teahouses, the simple lodges of Nepal: bedrooms and a shared dining room, which is the heart of the teahouse in the evenings. With us you sleep in twin rooms, and three meals a day, chosen from the teahouse menu, are included in the price. The large bag, up to 15 kg per person, is carried by the porters, and you walk with a daypack only.

What is not included are the extras the teahouses charge for separately: showers, internet, laundry and additional meals. Bring cash for these extras. Anyone who prefers a single room in the teahouses can add one for 20 dollars a night.

content.value: The Cho La pass and the Gokyo Lakes

Day 12 brings the most demanding walking day of the trek: crossing the Cho La pass, 5,420 m, between the Khumbu valley and the Gokyo valley. You leave Dzongla early, climb about 590 m to the pass and descend to Thagnak through a landscape of glaciers and lakes. You reach it after more than a week at high altitude, and it is a day of 10 to 11 hours. Conditions on the pass depend on the season and the weather, so the route may change at the discretion of the guides on the ground.

On the other side wait the Gokyo Lakes, a system of glacial lakes at 4,710 to 4,950 m, at the headwaters of the Dudh Koshi river. Above Gokyo village rises Gokyo Ri, 5,360 m, the second viewpoint of the trek over Everest and Lhotse, from which you also look down on the lakes themselves.

content.value: The Lukla flight, and the spare day

Lukla airport is considered one of the most challenging in the world because of its short runway, and flights stop whenever the weather does not allow them. In the busy seasons most regular flights to Lukla leave from the airport at Manthali in Ramechhap district, a few hours' drive from Kathmandu, not from Kathmandu itself.
Weather is the second challenge: cloud and fog can stop flights to and from Lukla for several days in a row, and sometimes helicopter flights too.

In our package the flights between Kathmandu and Lukla, in both directions, are by helicopter, so there is no need to drive to Manthali. A helicopter also depends on the weather, which is why we built one spare day in Kathmandu into the schedule before the flight home. If it is not needed, it becomes a free day in the city.
Permits and fees

To enter the area you need two permits: the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit and the entry permit of the local authority, Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality. The park permit costs 3,000 Nepalese rupees for foreign visitors, and the municipality fee has changed several times in recent years.
Both permits are included in the price of our trek, so you pay nothing on the trail. The Nepal visa is not included, and more on that below.

content.value: Visa for Nepal

Most visitors, including citizens of the UK, the EU, the US, Canada and Australia, get a tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. For a 19-day trip you need the 30-day visa, which costs 50 US dollars (as of 2026). Bring a passport valid for at least six months and the fee in cash. Rules can change, so check the official Nepal immigration website before you fly.
When to go
Nepal has two main trekking seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. The monsoon usually runs from June to the end of September, and sometimes lingers into early October.

During the monsoon months there are hardly any trekkers in the area, and in the fall it fills up. Our expeditions depart in spring and fall, and you will find the current dates on the expedition page.
How fit do you need to be

This is a trek, not a technical climb: there are no ropes and no ice axe. When there is snow on the trail, mainly at the Cho La pass, you walk in crampons. What it takes is endurance: the ability to walk 5 to 7 hours a day with a daypack, day after day, for two weeks, and more on the long days. The difficulty is cumulative, and altitude adds to it. We grade the trek as hard.

Previous trekking experience is not a requirement. If you can walk about 20 km a day, enjoy a challenge and come with strong motivation, the trek can suit you. The best preparation is long hikes with a pack in the months before departure. A medical certificate and health declaration are required from every participant, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join.

Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call. That way you reach Nepal with the right gear, already knowing the people you will walk with for two weeks.

Good to know: the trek is led by professional local guides from Nepal who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having.
What it costs and what is included

The Everest Base Camp and Gokyo trek costs 3,800 US dollars per person. It includes transfers between the airport and the hotel in Kathmandu, dinners at a restaurant before and after the trek, 3 nights in a 4-star hotel in Kathmandu in a single room with breakfast, domestic helicopter flights to Lukla and back, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms throughout the trek, all entry permits for the trek and Sagarmatha National Park, three meals a day from the menu, 2 liters of hot water a day, a shower and attached toilet where available on the route, professional local English-speaking guides, porters for personal gear up to 15 kg per person, a first aid kit carried by the guides, a pulse oximeter for the group and a satellite device, a personal area in the HighAir app, a personal gear checklist with an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide, and a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance, lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear, tips for guides and porters (250 dollars per person), the Nepal visa (50 dollars), vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and the extras the teahouses charge for separately, such as internet, laundry, alcohol and additional meals. A fourth hotel night in Kathmandu, if needed, is not included. A single room in the teahouses costs 20 dollars a night.

Before buying insurance, check that the policy covers trekking up to 5,545 m, including helicopter rescue. Note that in the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra nights, meals and flight changes, are the traveler's responsibility.
Everest Base Camp with HighAir

At HighAir we take groups to Everest Base Camp every year, in spring and fall. Our trek lasts 19 days, and deliberately so: they include two acclimatization days, a loop over the Cho La and through Gokyo, and a spare day. Groups are limited to 10 trekkers, and the success rate we publish for this route is 93 percent.
Anyone who comes back from Base Camp wanting more can think about the next step: a first summit above 6,000 m, such as Mera Peak or Island Peak in the same region.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber you see today on the summits of the world started once, on one mountain. If Everest is your mountain, even if only from its Base Camp, we are here.

content.value: Frequently asked questions
How many days does the Everest Base Camp trek take?

HighAir's trek, which also includes Kala Patthar, the Cho La pass and the Gokyo Lakes, lasts 19 days from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. 14 of them are on the trail, from landing in Lukla to getting back there, including two acclimatization days. There is also a preparation day in Kathmandu and a spare day in case of bad weather.
How hard is the Everest Base Camp trek?

We grade the trek as hard, but it is not technical: no ropes or ice axe, and crampons are needed only when there is snow on the trail. The difficulty is the altitude and the cumulative effort of two weeks of walking, 5 to 7 hours a day on most days. Previous experience is not required, but good fitness and a medical certificate are.
When is the best season for the Everest Base Camp trek?
Spring and fall, before and after the monsoon. The monsoon usually runs from June to September, and very few trekkers come to the area in those months. Our expeditions depart in spring and fall.
Can you see the summit of Everest from Base Camp?

You cannot see the summit from Base Camp itself. The best viewpoint is Kala Patthar, 5,545 m, which you climb the morning after Base Camp for sunrise facing Everest. Our route also has a second viewpoint, Gokyo Ri, 5,360 m.
Which permits do you need for the Everest Base Camp trek?

Two: the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit and the entry permit of the local authority, Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality. Both are included in the price of our trek, while the Nepal visa, 50 dollars for 30 days, is not.
Do I need a visa for Nepal?
Yes. Most visitors get a tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. A 30-day visa, enough for our 19-day trip, costs 50 US dollars (as of 2026).
